quotes.text: The song they're singing has the same melody as Jack Nitzsche's triumphant score, but it transfigures that score into sleepy, character-free waiting-room music.
After "Right Time Of The Night," Warnes found a niche as a singer of movie themes.

Aside from Cocker's gravel-filtered coffee growl, the real revelation here is Cocker's original backing group, the Grease Band, who are featured on a sublime version of "Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood."
This set is edgier and harder-rocking than most of Cocker's work with producer/arranger Leon Russell. Cocker is in full-on spastic mode through most of this, and it's fantastic.
This soulful sophomore effort features the Grease Band throughout as Leon Russell's production starts shifting toward what would eventually come to fruition on "Mad Dogs & Englishmen."
Cocker's versions of "The Letter," "She Came In Through The Bathroom Window," "Feelin' Alright," "Space Captain" and "Delta Lady" eclipsed the original versions and kept on going.

After "Mad Dogs & Englishmen," Cocker was never quite able to craft entire albums that were as consistent as his early releases. That said, Cocker never lost his voice and continued to score occasional hit singles and fan favorites for the rest of his career.
With his unique approach to songwriting and recording, and of course his uniquely gruff, bluesy voice, it's difficult to fully encapsulate the late Joe Cocker's legacy.

A crucial part of Cocker's discography was his sheer ingenuity in his covers, and the inclusion of such classic rearrangements as She Came In Through The Bathroom Window and You Can Leave Your Hat On is practically mandatory to the album.
